title: Protesters Question Trump’s Plan for a Huge Arch
summary:
Dozens of people protested at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, October 1, 2026. They opposed President Donald Trump’s plan for a 250-foot-tall arch. It would stand in a traffic circle on the bridge connecting the National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery.

Veterans, retirees and lawmakers attended. Speakers questioned the arch’s size, cost and location. They also said Congress had not approved it. They stood beside a tarp model they said was much smaller than the planned arch.

Jon Gundersen, a retired Army veteran and former Foreign Service officer, came from South Carolina. He is among the Vietnam War veterans suing the administration over the project. Public Citizen, the group leading the lawsuit, helped organize the protest.

Several speakers wanted veterans and their families to have more say. Senator Tammy Duckworth and other opponents said better services for veterans would honor them more.

The White House told NPR that the arch would improve cemetery visits and remind people of American heroes’ sacrifices.

Federal approval is still pending. At a Tuesday meeting, administration officials said they would keep the original plan. The National Capital Planning Commission is widely expected to consider it in early November.

A separate review about nearby protected landmarks ended early in the last week of September. The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation said it would send advice directly to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum by October 7. Charles Birnbaum of The Cultural Landscape Foundation criticized ending talks after only two meetings.

Some protesters want Congress to block federal funding. A Republican senator blocked a Democratic attempt earlier that week. November’s midterm elections could change control of Congress and affect the project starting in January. The lawsuit continues.
why_it_matters: The proposal raises questions about how to honor veterans, use government money and make decisions near protected landmarks. Its future remains uncertain.
